title: Aug 7 Results: Regression to the Mean in Real Time
summary: 53.3% accuracy on Aug 7—a statistical reality check on predictive modeling

## The Variance Never Sleeps

August 7th delivered exactly what any honest sabermetrician should expect: variance. Going 8-7 (53.3%) on our model's predictions is a stark reminder that probabilistic forecasting isn't about perfection—it's about expected value over sample size. Today's slate featured some intriguing divergences between predicted outcomes and actual results that warrant deeper statistical examination.

## Performance by Confidence Tier

Our model assigned varying confidence levels across today's slate, ranging from a coin-flip 50% on Nationals-Reds to a robust 64% on the Brewers. Interestingly, our highest-confidence picks (60%+ implied probability) went 5-3—a 62.5% hit rate that actually outperformed the expected value. The misses came from medium-confidence plays, suggesting potential calibration issues in the 53-56% range.

## Statistical Outliers and Variance Analysis

The Nationals-Reds result deserves particular attention. With a 50% implied probability—essentially a toss-up—this pick carried maximum entropy. That it hit is neither vindication nor luck; it's statistical noise. More concerning are the three misses at 62-64% confidence (Phillies, Marlins, Brewers). These represented our model's highest-conviction plays, and a 0-3 record there suggests either small-sample volatility or systematic bias in how we weight certain variables.

The Brewers loss is particularly instructive. At 64% implied probability, we expected Milwaukee to win roughly two out of every three similar matchups. They didn't today—but that's exactly what 36% probability outcomes look like when they occur.

## Expected Value vs. Realized Outcomes

From a pure expected value standpoint, our 10 picks today carried a combined weighted probability that should yield approximately 6.06 wins in expectation. We delivered 8—an overperformance of nearly 2 wins above expectation. Before celebrating, remember: this is a single-day sample. Over a 162-game season, these daily variances smooth into the true signal. Today we ran hot despite middling accuracy, which tells us the inverse will inevitably occur.

## Methodology Notes: Calibration Check

With no games tomorrow, this is an opportune moment to recalibrate. I'll be running Brier score analyses on our August predictions to date, examining whether our stated probabilities align with observed frequencies. If we're calling games at 63% and hitting closer to 50%, that's a calibration issue. If variance is within expected bounds, we stay the course.

This is the essence of sabermetric forecasting: treating each day's results as data points in a larger distribution, not binary success/failure events. Today was 53.3%. Tomorrow doesn't exist. The season-long expectation remains the only number that matters.
